An unambiguous autocrat holds the White House. Americans now fear not only the corruption of their municipal law enforcement, but the menace of a paramilitary force of racist thugs that owes allegiance only to the executive branch. Plutocrats work hand-in-glove with white nationalists, spies have penetrated the political press, and the government prosecutes dissenting speech as treason and threatens its opponents with deportation. The year, of course, is 1916.

The cartoonist Derf Backderf has a remarkable sense of which historical moment can be mined for unfamiliar parallels to the present day. His 2020 book, Kent State: Four Dead in Ohio, arrived perfectly timed to rebut disingenuous concerns over supposed campus-activist illiberalism; his 2012 My Friend Dahmer, about his high school friendship with future serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer, felt eerily attuned to a U.S. school culture traumatized by mass shootings.

An unambiguous autocrat holds the White House. Americans now fear not only the corruption of their municipal law enforcement, but the menace of a paramilitary force of racist thugs that owes allegiance only to the executive branch. Plutocrats work hand-in-glove with white nationalists, spies have penetrated the political press, and the government prosecutes dissenting speech as treason and threatens its opponents with deportation. The year, of course, is 1916.

The Dissidents: Autocrats! Vigilantes! Communists! And Cartoonists!, Derf Backderf, Harry N. Abrams, 344 pp., September 2026, $29.99

The cartoonist Derf Backderf has a remarkable sense of which historical moment can be mined for unfamiliar parallels to the present day. His 2020 book, Kent State: Four Dead in Ohio, arrived perfectly timed to rebut disingenuous concerns over supposed campus-activist illiberalism; his 2012 My Friend Dahmer, about his high school friendship with future serial killer Jeffrey Dahmer, felt eerily attuned to a U.S. school culture traumatized by mass shootings.

For his new graphic novel, The Dissidents: Autocrats! Vigilantes! Communists! And Cartoonists!, he has identified a doozy. The book is set among leftist cartoonists working in the small-but-fierce newsroom of The Masses, the Greenwich Village magazine that published cartoons, poetry, political essays, the occasional drawing by Picasso, and at least one interview with Lenin, and that sent John Reed to cover the Bolsheviks in Moscow in October 1917. It’s a comfortable milieu for Backderf, a veteran of the U.S. alternative press for which The Masses represents a kind of platonic ideal. While the book’s dialogue is largely invented, its research is impeccable. Every time I thought, “That can’t possibly be true,” I looked it up, and it was.

The life of The Masses was short: From 1911 to 1917, it was a leading organ of U.S. socialist thought, but after the passage of the Espionage Act of 1917, the U.S. Postal Service refused to deliver the magazine on the grounds that it was interfering with conscription. The publication shut down amid punitive prosecutions of its masthead and reconstituted as The Liberator, which was milder in tone. The new magazine was thus able to print Reed’s history-making dispatches; those articles would become the basis of his book Ten Days That Shook the World, arguably the most important document in English on the October Revolution.

Covers of The Masses and Liberator.Wikimedia Commons

The eyes through which Backderf shows us all this historical detail and contemporary resonance are those of Joe Hertle, a progressive artist working for the Newspaper Enterprise Association. Hertle is Backderf’s own creation, but the NEA is still around today, syndicating comic strips and stories of various kinds to papers around the United States. Backderf imagines Hertle as a low-ranking cartoonist there, only in his mid-20s when the story takes place. He’s interested in the burgeoning labor movement—early on in the story, he loses his leg below the knee to a trolley car during a riot. But he’s also fascinated by the brilliance of the artists publishing in The Masses, which turns out some of the most beautiful U.S. artwork of the period with their illustrations and cartoons, all while dogged by a bloodlust that seems to have infected their whole society.

Backderf has an enviable array of artists to defend the radical politics he explores here. Foremost is probably Art Young, a brilliant cartoonist who clashed with his less didactically minded colleagues. “They want to run pictures of ash cans and girls hitching up their skirts in Horatio Street,” he groused in 1916, “regardless of ideas and without title.” Those colleagues were John Sloan and George Bellows, and they took the name of the Ash Can School from Young’s potshot. There’s something transcendent in the way Backderf contextualizes and reproduces obscure illustrations by future luminaries alongside Harry Ryle Hopps’ famous “Destroy This Mad Brute” military recruitment poster. What, after all, is Bellows without his comrades in the socialist press and his contemporaries in the broadsheets?

Joe Hertle, the fictional protagonist of The Dissidents, finds little sympathy for his politics in Woodrow Wilson’s United States.Abrams Books

In many respects, The Dissidents is a bracing remedial education. The villain of the piece is Woodrow Wilson, a U.S. president who is traditionally celebrated for leading the country onto the global stage during World War I and for his own academic work as a historian and president of Princeton University.

But Backderf, drawing on Adam Hochschild’s recent history of the period, American Midnight, as well as contemporaneous accounts, contends convincingly that we ignore the domestic character of Wilson’s government at our peril. He was, after all, a fervent racist who screened D.W. Griffith’s The Birth of a Nation at the White House and immediately allowed the expansion of government office segregation upon taking office—this after plying Black leaders with promises of moderation.

Wilson signed the notorious Sedition Act of 1918 and the aforementioned Espionage Act, which still plagues U.S. civil libertarians with its layers of secrecy, obfuscation, impunity, and good old bureaucratic busywork. More importantly (for Backderf’s purposes), he started a censorship board for editorial cartoonists called the Bureau of Cartoons. The bureau enlisted popular illustrators to sell the idea of censorship to their peers: One guidelines pamphlet boasted a cover by no less an eminence than James Montgomery Flagg, of the now-iconic “I Want You” poster.

Academics need to get better at reaching non-experts. Narrative media offer one possibility.

The most striking contemporary analogue in The Dissidents is that of the American Protective League, a consortium of violent goons whose existence was approved by Wilson and which was allowed to operate under color of law, despite being a club of bullies little better than the Ku Klux Klan. With Wilson’s imprimatur, they waged undeclared war on pacifists and conscientious objectors, raiding businesses and conducting arrests at their own discretion. During one three-day period in 1918, they were even allowed to conduct draft card checks throughout New York City and arrest supposed dodgers—as well as those who simply forgot to carry their draft cards with them.

In this era, too, to my surprise, segregation enthusiasts were using the not-quite-a-slur “hyphenated Americans” to refer to people who had the temerity to bring along some of their own culture when they moved to the United States. (I’ve been hearing U.S. conservatives try for laughs with this one since the 1990s.) Emma Goldman’s deportation at the end of the book feels inevitable.

All of it seems eerily similar to the 2024 Republican National Convention and its signs urging “mass deportation now” and to the work of the Department of Homeland Security’s militarized enforcement arms—Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Homeland Security Investigations, and Customs and Border Patrol. But Backderf places all of these familiar organizations and characters in a context so meticulously drawn—both historically and with his pen—that The Dissidents is a vivid evocation of an entire period, not just the parts that invite contemporary comparisons.

That evocation comes primarily through the art history in The Dissidents, a genuinely wonderful contribution to our shared understanding of the period. Backderf’s own style is deliberately prosaic, with lots of heavy black ink, but the artists he’s chosen for his cast of characters often use a black crayon, and Backderf includes stats of their cartoons on his own pages; these bring forth a whole range of values seen nowhere else in the book’s world.

Joe admires the provocative political cartoons in The Masses.Abrams Books

Backderf takes great pains to dramatize all the different layers of artistic expression available to the general public during World War I, and how they changed in response to social pressures. To avoid seeming too sympathetic to the Germans, The Katzenjammer Kids and Hans und Fritz, both created by Rudolph Dirks, were renamed The Shenanigan Kids and The Captain and the Kids, respectively.

Cartoonist Art Young drew scathing indictments of capitalism, official impunity, and even the Associated Press; he was charged under the Espionage Act and put on trial, through which he snoozed defiantly. Other Masses contributors weren’t as lucky: For organizing French railway workers to strike, Robert Minor was imprisoned abroad by the U.S. military and narrowly avoided being executed; Maurice Becker, arrested for being a conscientious objector, was held and tortured at the United States Disciplinary Barracks in Fort Leavenworth, a military prison in Kansas.

The rest of the press seemed to consider these men to have gotten off easy. “We are now at war, and militant pacifists are earnestly reminded that there is no shortage of hemp or lamp-posts,” snarled the Wall Street Journal in a bravely unbylined front-page editorial on April 6, the day the United States formally entered the war. This, too, evokes more recent memories of the U.S. press disciplining its less hawkish members. (The Journal recently published an letter under the delightfully petulant headline “The Iran War Isn’t Deranged.”)

Undergirding the eeriness of its parallels, depending on how depressed you’ve been lately, you might find in The Dissidents a sense of relief. I certainly did. It’s not that things aren’t terrible, but it’s worth remembering that they’ve been bad before and gotten better (and worse) as the passage of time has done its thing. If it’s not exactly a comfort to feel that somewhere in the U.S. character there lurks a penchant for thuggery, it is at least nice to think that, for long periods, its expression has been curbed and limited. “Things don’t last forever, Joe,” the great, subtle artist Cornelia Barns tells our hero, as the net begins to tighten around the radical journalists of The Masses. And that’s true enough, for good and for ill.

#5939. Longtime West Virginia Sen. Rockefeller dies

Former Sen. Jay Rockefeller, a five-term West Virginia Democrat and champion for the rural poor, has died at the age of 89.

Rockefeller, who retired after the 2014 elections, played key roles on the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee, where he helped write landmark children’s health insurance legislation, as well as the Commerce, Science and Transportation and Intelligence panels which he chaired.

A staunchly progressive lawmaker, he represented a deeply conservative state that turned further to the right in his later years. Rockefeller, scion of a famous New York family renowned for its wealth, never wavered in his convictions and retired rather than face a potential backlash from voters upset by the then-Obama administration’s attempts to rein in the coal industry.

Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who challenged Rockefeller for his seat before he decided not to seek reelection, released a statement Friday praising her predecessor’s legacy.

“Jay dedicated his life to serving West Virginia and our nation, leaving a lasting legacy. He was always a true gentleman who treated me with respect, kindness, and encouragement,” Capito said. “Over the years, we developed a wonderful friendship that transcended politics, and I will always be grateful for that.”

West Virginia’s Republican Gov. Patrick Morrisey — himself a transplanted Northerner, with roots in Brooklyn and New Jersey — lauded Rockefeller’s record on health care and aid for coal miners and veterans in their adopted state.

“His work helped shape our state and left a lasting mark on the lives of generations of West Virginians,” Morrisey said.

Rockefeller was born in Manhattan, NY on June 18, 1937, the great-grandson of Standard Oil Co. founder John D. Rockefeller, who was once considered the world’s richest man. Rockefeller attended Harvard University, graduating with an A.B. in 1961, but his passion was for the far-east and spent three years studying at the International Christian University in Tokyo.

He returned to the states and was appointed by President John F. Kennedy to the National Advisory Council of the Peace Corps in 1961, spearheaded the Peace Corps initial program in the Philippines. He worked for a brief time in what was then known as U.S. Department of Far Eastern Affairs before deciding to embark on a public service role of a more personal nature. He enrolling as a VISTA volunteer, in the program which would later be known as Americorps, and moved to the small mining community of Emmons, West Virginia in 1964 at age 27.

In West Virginia, Rockefeller found his life’s work. He described the experience as being “reborn,” and spoke often the poverty and hardship he encountered living in the small town. “I could not leave,” he said of West Virginia. “I [had] become so devoted to those people and the unfairness.

He had planned to stay only one year, but decided to stay and became active in local politics. He broke from his family’s long tradition of Republican loyalty and ran successfully for the House of Delegates as a Democrat in 1966. Two years later, he was elected Secretary of State.

Rockefeller lost a bid for governor in 1972, but he became the president of West Virginia Wesleyan College and continued to place roots in the state. He married Sharon Percy Rockefeller in 1967 and they started their family. When he ran for governor again in 1976, he won, and served two terms before winning election to the U.S. Senate in 1984, ultimately serving five terms before retiring in 2014.

Rockefeller was determined to increase economic opportunities for West Virginia, for whom he felt was forgotten and abandoned by the rest of the country. He called the people of his state “ the hardest working people I know,” and believed that bringing more business opportunities would help lift the state out of severe rural poverty and the dependence on the coal industry.

Rockefeller traveled to Japan and worked tirelessly to bring a Toyota manufacturing plant to Buffalo, W.Va, one of over twenty Japanese companies he’d brought to West Virginia. He fought for fair trade policies and targeted tax relief to protect West Virginia industries such as steel and chemicals.

Coal mining had long been the economic backbone of West Virginia, but Rockefeller felt more must be done to protect miners, many of whom worked in unsafe conditions or fell ill with Pneumoconiosis, or Black Lung Disease, after years of inhaling coal dust.

But defying the coal industry came with a political cost. When Rockefeller originally ran for governor in 1972, he had opposed mountaintop mining, also called strip mining, or the practice of removing large amounts of earth and rock in order to access underground seams of coal. When he ran again in 1976, he reversed his position and won.

But even as he ascended to the Senate, Rockefeller remained both friend and foe to the coal industry.

Despite growing up on the Upper East Side of Manhattan, figuratively and literally hundreds of miles away from coal mines, Rockefeller understood its deep roots in West Virginia’s economy and culture. He believed it was the miners — rather than industry — for whom he was defending.

He hung a century-old photo of a coal miner in his Senate office in Hart, and would point to the photo and remark to visitors that “this is why I’m here and who I work for.”

Rockefeller fought to secure pensions for miners, especially as coal companies would file for bankruptcy and immediately restructure to do away with pension plans.

In 1990, Rockefeller was one of only 11 senators to vote against the bipartisan Clean Air Act, which he felt disadvantaged workers in West Virginia. But those close to him said the decision weighed heavily on him, and Rockefeller privately worried that the lack of such regulations would pollute the air and destroy waterways, the brunt of which would be born by the same disadvantaged people whom he vowed to protect.

He believed strongly in the deliberative aspects of the legislative process, consuming great amounts of reading material to familiarize himself with the issues. During a time of increasing partisan rancor, Rockefeller still reached across the aisle to find a willing partner, even when there was not one to be found.

In 2010, as the Environmental Protection Agency’s greenhouse gas regulations were coming to fruition, Rockefeller came up with a compromise to delay implementation for two years.

He viewed himself as a broker between industry interests and the hard working people from coal-states like West Virginia. He had hoped that his years of standing up for coal miners and West Virginia interests would foster enough goodwill among industries primed to oppose any compromise that was less than an all-out rejection of the existing EPA statutes.

But industry walked away from Rockefeller, preferring a hard-line opposition to EPA regulations, and lobbied other senators to vote against Rockefeller’s measure. Furious, Rockefeller took to the floor of the U.S. Senate to denounce the coal industry and its leaders, an unprecedented action for a popular coal-state senator.

“The reality is that many who run the coal industry today would rather attack false enemies and deny real problems then find solutions,” he said on the Senate floor on June 19, 2013 . “Scare tactics are a cynical waste of time, money and, worst of all, coal miners’ hopes. But sadly, these coal operators have closed themselves off from any other opposing voices and few dared to speak out for change — even though it’s been staring them in the face for years.”

His fury against the coal industry was heard loudly, many speculating that he would retire rather than face re-election.

He had won re-election to the Senate handedly during his five campaigns. In 2008, his final election, he was re-elected with nearly 64 percent of the vote. But six months following his fated coal speech, in January 2013, Rockefeller announced he would retire at the end of his fifth term.

Rockefeller’s legacy may best be known for his fight to expand health care for vulnerable populations, including children, the economically disadvantaged and the elderly. Rockefeller served as one of the chief congressional champions for President Bill Clinton’s proposed health care overhaul, later he played a critical role and was a loud progressive voice in writing and passing the Affordable Care Act in the Senate.

Rockefeller believed strongly in a public health insurance option, offering it as an amendment in the Senate Finance Committee during the ACA markup. A public-run insurance plan, he said, would put patients before profits, and help those people, especially West Virginians, with high healthcare costs and poor coverage who were left “out in the cold.”

“These are people,” Rockefeller said, visibly emotional during his closing arguments to the Senate Finance Committee. “Eleven-year-old kids. These are families, and we have to respect them. And you respect them by giving them a choice.”

The amendment failed. Rockefeller pivoted to strengthen Medicaid and Children’s Health Insurance Program provisions, believing that poor and disadvantaged families could seek refuge within those programs. CHIP had been one of Rockefeller’s signature legislative victories, helping to write that program initially in 1997 and later working on a major expansion that became law in 2009.

Despite his initial concerns and later disappointments — at one time saying publicly he could not support ACA as it stood — he later brought his support, citing it as a win for all Americans and actively lobbied his colleagues to support it.

Rockefeller was also known for his role on the Senate Intelligence Committee. A former chairman, he was critical of the nation’s mismanagement of the Iraq war and clashed frequently with Republicans over the treatment of detainees. After he retired from Congress, Rockefeller served as a distinguished fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.

Respect for Rockefeller ran deep on Capitol Hill. He was beloved by staff and known as a thoughtful, deliberative lawmaker. He had a fondness for classical music and served as a board member of the Bach Consort, an organization in Washington devoted to the study and performance of the music of Bach and his contemporaries. He admired art and Asian culture, and served as a board member of the Asia Society. He was known as a man dedicated to his work and his adopted state of West Virginia.

Rockefeller is survived by his wife, Sharon Percy Rockefeller, four children: John (Emily) Rockefeller V; Valerie (Steven) Wayne; Charles Rockefeller; and Justin (Indre) Rockefeller; and nine grandchildren.

Disclosure: the author served as a staffer in Rockefeller’s Senate office from 2009-2011.

Was it the Iran war? Corruption? The cost of living? Data centers? By now, everyone has a pet theory to explain why the Democrats flipped both the House and the Senate—and why voters rebuked U.S. President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. What matters now is how the two sides interpret the results and navigate the political battles to come. And broadly, how the world reacts to the shifting political landscape in the United States.

On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Susan Glasser, a staff writer at the New Yorker and the former editor in chief of Foreign Policy. The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

Was it the Iran war? Corruption? The cost of living? Data centers? By now, everyone has a pet theory to explain why the Democrats flipped both the House and the Senate—and why voters rebuked U.S. President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. What matters now is how the two sides interpret the results and navigate the political battles to come. And broadly, how the world reacts to the shifting political landscape in the United States.

On the latest episode of FP Live, I spoke with Susan Glasser, a staff writer at the New Yorker and the former editor in chief of Foreign Policy. The full interview is available on the video box atop this page, or on the FP Live podcast on Spotify, YouTube, or Apple. What follows here is a lightly edited transcript.

Ravi Agrawal: I want to start with the big picture. You wrote in your last column: “For now and for forever, the midterm election of 2026 will be known as one of the most decisive rejections of an American president.” Say more.

Susan Glasser: You have to go very far back in history to see a result this explicit, loud, and across-the-board. A lot of people have been comparing it to the post-Watergate elections of 1974 and 1976. If you look at the popular vote, it is the widest midterm margin for Democrats since 1976. Right now, they are trending toward a 13-percentage-point advantage.

However, if you look at the consequences in Congress and how many seats Democrats picked up, you actually have to go much farther back in time to find an election that was this decisive of a swing to either party. The last time this happened was in 1946 and 1948. You have a more than 35-seat pickup for Democrats in the House of Representatives—so far—and as much as an eight-seat pickup in the Senate. That combined House and the Senate pickup hasn’t been seen since the postwar era in American politics.

What’s different about this election compared to other recent ones, such as the 1994 wave that brought Republicans to power in Congress, is that it is a campaign centered around the person of the president, his policies, his leadership, and what he had done with his party. That’s what makes this result so resounding and impactful.

RA: Not in my lifetime have I seen states like Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Texas come into play in this way for a blue wave.

Many of us were quite stunned to see a post on X from U.S. Vice President J.D. Vance the morning after the election, not only for its speed, but for its analysis. He said, quite simply, “The reason we lost is the [Iran] war.” Do you agree with that?

SG: That was an amazing document. It is pretty much without modern precedent, and I think we have only begun to see what the ramifications of that will be. U.S. President Donald Trump has yet to respond to it, but for a man who has remade the executive branch of the federal government around the single criterion of blind loyalty to him, to have his own vice president attack his signature policy is … wow.

RA: It’s notable that as reporters have looked at how the Iran war has played out in the White House, Vance tends to emerge as the person who was most against the war. He himself is probably the source for many of those claims, so we should take them with a grain of salt, right?

SG: Vance, according to himself, was nobly against this war that is extremely unpopular with the American public. We’re seeing a number of factors at play here. One, Vance is desperately trying to see if there is a path forward for him to run for president in 2028. Two, you will see a number of Republican officeholders and MAGA pundit types like Sean Hannity climbing aboard this argument that it was just the Iran war that lost them the election, because it absolves them of some of the other catastrophes that Trump has wrought on the American public. It’s a convenient foil for them if they can try to win the battle of the narrative around what just happened here.

In my view, the Iran war and the subsequent spike in prices was quite disastrous for Trump and the Republicans politically. However, I believe that this election is a broader repudiation of the Trump administration. That is part of what Vance and Hannity and others are trying to head off.

RA: I agree with you, but just to play devil’s advocate for a minute here: One of the things I think Vance was getting at is that when voters, especially the people who supported Trump in 2024, voted for the Trump campaign’s version of America First, part of that bargain was that there would be no more wars. There’s an argument then that what they really want is just less foreign policy.

The other point to make is that if affordability is the one big-ticket item, which is connected to everything we’re discussing at some level—certainly the Iran war, certainly the tariffs—then how much of what we’ve just seen this week is a secular problem of people swinging from one party to another because they’re unhappy with the current economic conditions? Or how much of it do you think is going to be attributed to the Trump administration’s very unique policies and Trump’s persona?

SG: In politics, as in life, if you start lying to yourself and believing it, you’re in big trouble. Republicans may well come up with an explanation for this election. If it’s a wrong one, or a BS one, they’re going to pay future political consequences.

If you look at a recent Wall Street Journal survey and a number of others, the top issue many Americans said they were bringing to the polls with them wasn’t affordability but corruption. Vance isn’t going to talk about corruption, but we are witnessing the looting of the American presidency on a massive scale. The self-enrichment of our president and a small coterie of his family and other insiders defies all precedent in American history. It’s not partisan to say that people in Kansas are probably pretty offended by the idea of the president of the United States making more than $2 billion off of the presidency in his first year back in office. He himself has admitted it. In an interview earlier this year, he said that he tried to follow the rules—which he didn’t—and it turned out nobody cared.

Corruption has been a powerful force in this election, as it has been in a number of other recent elections this year. The Hungarian election that ousted [Prime Minister] Viktor Orban is one good example, but there are a lot of others. My no. 1 explanation for this election outcome would be the perceived and actual self-enrichment of this out-of-touch leader and his disinterest in the concerns of the electorate around their own economic situation. It encompasses a lot of issues, including taking the country to war. That’s not how our system is supposed to work, for the president to be so disdainful of the country that he doesn’t even feel a need to explain to them why he went to war. There will have to be some fallout from the election.

It wasn’t just Iran. Israel, tariffs, and immigration also loomed large in voters’ minds.

From the Iran war to boat strikes to Ukraine, Democrats now have powerful leverage.

RA: Let’s talk about what next. I’m curious how you think Democrats are going to use this majority in the House and the Senate. What are the topics and items you think they’re going to pursue in their first few months, knowing full well that Trump has already posted on Truth Social an image of a red cap with the word “VETO” on it? There are limits to what they can do, but what are they going to try?

SG: They may be recalibrating because the scale of their victory is so big. I had a conversation a few weeks ago with Chris Coons, who’s going to be the new chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. At that time, he was hopeful that the Democrats would win the majority, but he certainly didn’t think they would have 55 seats. What Democrats may be able to do with 55 seats and a number of centrist Democrats coming in from places like Kansas, North Carolina, and Texas is a different ball game.

The first stop for Democrats looking to affect national security and foreign policy is appropriations bills and the power of the purse. They can attach policy riders on a must-pass defense authorization bill or put provisions into appropriations bills that outline how money can and cannot be spent. Those are things we definitely will see, especially because there’s a real bipartisan consensus, in particular on Ukraine.

I think we will see, at a minimum, much more aggressive efforts to stop Trump from switching sides in the war. I could see some of those very questionable deals that are being discussed between special envoy Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, and the Russians—business deals with Russian entities that might enrich Trump insiders and that no American companies actually want—being a quick casualty of this midterm election result.

RA: I’m imagining that the Kremlin is not going to be looking at these results and smiling. I’m sure they’re a bit worried, although simultaneously it’s also clear that Ukraine needs America less today than it did two years ago. They’re trying to become more resilient, and they’re looking at this election quite warily.

I’m curious how you read this election when it comes to shifting attitudes toward Israel, which just had its own elections. What does it mean for broader U.S. foreign policy in the Middle East?

SG: There is a backlash in both parties, interestingly, about Trump’s embrace of [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu and Israel in such an unequivocal way. That’s some of the tone, certainly, of the kind of emergent Vance wing of the party (to the extent there is a Vance wing). There is definitely a backlash in both parties about America’s traditional commitment to Israel in the face of how Netanyahu has prosecuted a scorched-earth war with the Palestinians. That’s true for Democrats in a very dramatic way.

Let’s wait and see what the consequences of Israel’s recent election are. Let’s not forget that they just voted to reject Netanyahu. But given the particularities of that system and his incredible ability to survive, we’ll have to wait and see. Whether Netanyahu or someone else is leading Israel will affect the politics here in Washington.

It’s the Gulf Arabs who have been the engines of a lot of Trump’s foreign policy, not to mention the piggy banks for him and his family. Somebody said to me recently that all the things that we suspect are happening between Putin’s Russia and Trump actually are happening—in terms of vast amounts of sums being directed to Trump and his family—from Gulf interests.

But I think the Gulf Arabs are also very unhappy with Trump. They’re finding out what many others have found out: that Trump doesn’t view relationships as mutual and loyalty is a one-way street with him. Not that long ago, a very senior official from the Middle East asked me: “Why do we have all these American bases and buy all this American military technology to protect ourselves if in fact it’s now the reason that we’re at war? What’s the point of paying the protection money?” It suggests we are at a larger pivot point in the Middle East in terms of geopolitics and the alliances than escaping this narrow quagmire with Iran would suggest. We’re likely looking at a rearrangement of a lot of things in the Middle East in the next two years.

RA: I’m curious how you are thinking about what comes next from the Democratic Party’s side. We’ve all been noting how they won with a very broad tent. There’s a broad slate of candidates, from a Methodist minister in Kansas to a Muslim doctor in Michigan. Are you beginning to detect some coalescing around a coherent foreign policy for the Democrats at this point, or is that a long ways away?

SG: The short answer is “no.” Will Rogers said it a long time ago: “I’m not a member of any organized political party, I’m a Democrat.” Democrats are by definition the more big-tent party in American politics, and they have leaned into that in recent years. Trump spent the last two years campaigning against the very idea of diversity as a strength. So there are some coherent principles that separate these two parties.

Democrats do not have one single coherent view. [Former President Joe] Biden was a backward-looking president in many ways, including with respect to foreign policy. He believed in the possibility of returning to a status quo ante, as a man who was shaped by the foreign-policy debates of the Cold War and perceived threats, opportunities, and alliances through that lens. So there’s a generational shift that’s taking place. I think you’ll see much younger Democratic presidential candidates in 2028. There is also a radical shift in the Senate. This is something people haven’t paid enough attention to. A huge percentage of the Senate is turning over, a much higher percentage than is normal. I think we’re looking at nearly 20 new senators, and the average age of those senators is somewhere in the 50s, and as compared with the average of the people who just left, who would be well into their post-retirement years if they were anybody other than a politician. So a generational shift is definitely going to have consequences on the foreign-policy orientation of the Democrats.

RA: It’s quite literally out with the old.

One thing that we haven’t touched on yet is how this past week could be seen as a repudiation of all the things you’ve said, but also of Big Tech. Elon Musk is the other big loser from this week. He literally poured hundreds of millions of dollars into campaigns, and voters have been quite clear: They’ve rejected data centers. They’ve supported candidates who promised regulation.

SG: It is incredible. Five hundred million dollars is more money than has ever been spent on any election by an individual in the history of ours or any country, by a large order of magnitude. That obscene amount of money produced literally zero victories for him. It’s a remarkable moment. It’s one that will be studied. It happened to play right into a campaign theme that Democrats already had across the country, which is a kind of populism of the center slash center-left. It’s this idea that billionaires and a small circle of oligarchic crony capitalists were conspiring with Trump to make sure that they face no legislative or regulatory roadblocks to reinventing the future however they wanted to and in their own self-interest. So this obscene amount of money came at the exact moment when it was already the message for many Democrats around the country.

Does it mean the new Democratic Congress is going to join hands with the Trump administration and regulate artificial intelligence? I’m going to say “no,” in part because the Democratic Congress, as well as the Republican Congress, opted out of any meaningful regulation in the last round of tech innovation in the era of the internet. They basically punted. They talked and talked and never did anything in a meaningful sense. So I’m very pessimistic about major legislation. But I think this could be probably a defining issue, if not the defining issue in the 2028 presidential election. We may be talking a lot less about Trump and a lot more about AI.

Ravi Agrawal is the editor in chief of Foreign Policy. X: @RaviReports

#5937. Can the Nordic Model Save NATO?

Since its founding in 1922, Foreign Affairs has been the leading forum for serious discussion of American foreign policy and global affairs. The magazine has featured contributions from many leading international affairs experts.

MATTI PESU is Senior Research Fellow in the Finland and Northern European Security Research Program at the Finnish Institute of International Affairs.

In August, at Finland’s request, the Swedish government deployed fighter aircraft and a warship to help patrol Finland’s eastern airspace and the Gulf of Finland against Russian air incursions and drones straying from Ukrainian operations. Critically, the Swedish assets involved were placed under Finnish command and followed Finnish rules of engagement. It was the latest example of how Finland and Sweden, the two newest additions to NATO, have made qualitative leaps in defense coordination.

The Nordic countries have expanded regional collaboration significantly in the past four years. Between them, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and Sweden now boast a new long-term defense strategy, a cross-border transit area, frequent joint exercises, and unprecedented levels of command integration. In effect, these governments are forming their own regional deterrence cluster: a like-minded group of states deepening military cooperation to strengthen deterrence and, if required, ensure NATO’s broader collective defense.

The Nordic model offers a glimpse of the adaptive solutions that may sustain NATO through uncertain times. Moscow’s appetite for risk is growing; its military buildup and escalating attacks on European infrastructure suggest that Russia constitutes a long-term threat to the alliance. At the same time, the Trump administration is pushing its European allies to take primary responsibility for the continent’s defense. Europeans must therefore deter a more dangerous Russia with less help.

To strengthen their deterrence and defense capabilities, member states along NATO’s extended frontline—and in the Baltic and Black Sea regions, in particular—should build their own regional clusters and foster a strong latticework of bilateral and “minilateral” partnerships with their neighbors. Regionalization remains a taboo subject among most of the alliance’s political leadership; NATO is, after all, a collective defense alliance founded on indivisible security. But regional efforts at the military level will both make NATO more effective and advance the United States’ vision of a more European NATO.

Nordic-style deterrence clusters are thus a win-win. Yet in its erratic, occasionally aggressive approach to Greenland and the North Atlantic, Washington has risked undercutting the very allies that are delivering what it wants. The United States should use the recently signed Greenland deal as a reset to embrace Nordic defense efforts and create incentives for other allies to follow suit.

Nordic defense collaboration took its current institutional form in 2009, when recession-era budgetary constraints pushed the region’s five countries to rethink their defense commitments. Finland and Sweden joined NATO members Denmark, Iceland, and Norway in establishing the Nordic Defense Cooperation, primarily in hopes of cutting procurement costs. NORDEFCO boasted some early wins, including cross-border air force training in the uncongested airspace of northern Finland, Norway, and Sweden. But because NORDEFCO spanned NATO members and nonallied states, bureaucratic hurdles and a lenient threat environment quickly sapped momentum from joint procurement.

Only after Russia’s 2014 invasion of Ukraine did some Nordic countries begin to see cooperation as a security imperative, not just a way to save money. Finland and Sweden launched a no-limits military partnership that included joint wartime planning. And Norway, despite maintaining its NATO-first approach, gradually embraced operational cooperation with its two non-NATO neighbors in times of crisis. By 2020, when the countries signed a trilateral statement of intent, they were conducting extensive joint exercises, sharing intelligence on common threats, and discussing their national defense plans with an eye toward coordinated crisis response.

Any remaining limits on Nordic military cooperation evaporated once Finland and Sweden joined NATO following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, in 2022. The region’s five countries agreed that Moscow posed an urgent security threat to themselves and to Europe as a whole. Even Denmark, which was previously reticent about regional collaboration, warmed to collective defense efforts. In 2023, it joined Finland, Norway, and Sweden in developing the Nordic Airpower Concept, which will give them the ability to fight as one force with their combined 250 advanced fighter aircraft. Denmark has also pledged to contribute personnel to the Swedish-led Forward Land Forces Finland, the NATO battle group that rotates between northern Finland and Sweden. When Denmark served as chair of NORDEFCO in 2024, the five governments also signed NORDEFCO Vision 2030, which outlines their ambition for joint operations that are aligned with both national and NATO defense interests. To support the logistical underpinnings of land force cooperation, the initiative established a seamless, borderless Nordic military mobility corridor.

A division of labor is now emerging: Finland commands regional land operations, Norway hosts the regional headquarters for air operations, and Sweden is becoming the logistics hub and transit area for joint military operations in northern Europe. Denmark, for its part, hosts a regional headquarters for special operations. The Nordic deterrence cluster also functions smoothly within NATO’s collective defense framework. Larger NATO allies—including France, Germany, the United Kingdom, and the United States—routinely operate and exercise in the Nordic space alongside their regional partners and fill capability gaps in areas such as intelligence, reconnaissance, and surveillance. The result is an increase in defense capabilities in NATO’s Joint Operations Area Northwest, which covers the North Atlantic and includes vital sea-lanes, critical undersea infrastructure, and the Arctic and Nordic regions bordering Russian strategic hot spots.

Deterrence clusters could well be the future of NATO’s frontline posture. In addition to NATO’s Joint Operations Area Northwest, NATO has two more regional plans—Center, covering the Baltic states and central Europe, and Southeast, covering Turkey and the Balkans—each with its own operations area and command center network. Governments in these two regions should follow the Nordic example and take the initiative to strengthen their own minilateral ties within the NATO framework.

An obvious starting point is the southeastern Baltic Sea, which sits at the heart of NATO’s Joint Operations Area Center. Although the Baltic states have a shared vulnerability to Russian encroachment, defense cooperation has been modest since they joined NATO, with Estonia, Latvia, and Lithuania preferring to rely on extraregional patrons such as the United States. Recent moves, however, suggest that regional collaboration is gathering pace: Estonia and Latvia have jointly procured the IRIS-T air defense system, and all three countries are coordinating their HIMARS rocket systems and building the Baltic Defense Line, a fortification project designed to channel, delay, and block a Russian ground invasion.

But Baltic cooperation would benefit from a more comprehensive minilateral layer resembling NORDEFCO. In practice, this could mean coordinating national defense plans, conducting joint exercises, and sharing missile stocks for air defense systems. It could also entail merging HIMARS launchers for joint fires capability, better integrating national contributions to the Baltic Defense Line, and jointly operating uncrewed vessels to monitor the sea and underwater infrastructure. The aim would be to enable three militaries to fight together as seamlessly as possible, generating a combined power greater than the sum of its parts.

Such a format, if realized, should also involve Poland—an emerging European military powerhouse that currently plays a limited role in Baltic defense. Although Warsaw maintains a relatively robust defense partnership with Lithuania, involving joint exercises and working groups, the two neighbors have previously failed to establish a joint exercise area in the Suwalki Gap, a key strategic corridor and vulnerable supply line connecting the Baltic states to continental Europe. A stronger minilateral framework would create a standing process for joint planning and consultation that could resolve the local objections and divergent strategic priorities that have dogged previous negotiations over the gap.

Within such a framework, Warsaw could reinforce regional defense by connecting its East Shield—Poland’s own program of fortifications, barriers, and surveillance systems along its borders with Russia and Belarus—with the Baltic Defense Line and by contributing ground-based air defenses to NATO’s Baltic Air Policing mission. The fundamental aim should be to strengthen Poland’s role as a leading security provider in the Baltic region alongside Germany, which is permanently stationing a brigade in Lithuania.

The other frontline arena that would most benefit from a deterrence cluster is the Black Sea region, which sits within NATO’s Joint Operations Area Southeast. Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey have struggled to cooperate because of divergent assessments of the threat posed by Russia. Building minilateral latticework here is clearly harder than in the Nordic or Baltic Sea areas. But in a more European NATO, the rest of the alliance would expect Black Sea allies to contribute more to collective defense, and the conditions for doing so are improving.

The most promising domain for expanded minilateral cooperation is maritime. In July 2024, Bulgaria, Romania, and Turkey launched a joint mine-clearing operation, which led to the establishment of a joint mission to protect energy infrastructure, telecommunications networks, and undersea pipelines owned and operated by the three allies. This embryonic naval force could be developed further to cover more ambitious contingencies in the Black Sea, from sea surveillance to the protection of territorial integrity, as the Finnish-Swedish naval task force does in the Baltic Sea.

Air forces are another potentially fruitful area for Nordic-style collaboration, especially as regional militaries grow their capabilities. Bulgaria awaits its F-16s, Romania is set to acquire F-35s, and Turkey, already a potent air power, is seeking readmission to the F-35 program. In 2009, the Nordic air forces began weekly cross-border training, paving the way for today’s cooperation. More frequent exercises among the Black Sea allies would be a logical first step toward enhancing interoperability.

For the Nordics, reaching today’s level of collaboration took more than 15 years. Other frontline regions cannot afford to wait that long. Russia may emerge from the war in Ukraine more capable and less risk averse. Tighter subregional cooperation would not only benefit the security of exposed allies on the frontline by enhancing their capacity to respond together. It would also make NATO’s frontline posture more effective, deterring Russian encroachment deeper into Europe—an aim that allies farther from the frontline should share. Moreover, by strengthening the minilateral latticework, countries close to Russia would enhance their capacity to act together before NATO acted collectively. In extreme circumstances, if the alliance was paralyzed, subregional clusters would offer a hedge, enabling frontline allies to respond together.

The United States, too, has a vested interest in the development of deterrence clusters across NATO’s eastern borderlands. U.S. officials have articulated a vision for “NATO 3.0,” a rebalanced alliance in which Europeans lead their own conventional defense and the United States plays a supporting role, providing extended nuclear deterrence and a few other capabilities. If the Europeans are to assume primary responsibility for their conventional defense, subregional cooperation arrangements—with high interoperability, joint procurement, planning and command capacity, cross-border mobility, and even certain divisions of labor—will be paramount.

Nordic defense cooperation represents the most mature version of such efforts, and the Nordic states have already demonstrated their readiness to work with the United States on Russian-related security threats. Finland and Norway, for instance, have directed their intelligence capabilities toward monitoring what happens on the Russian side of their borders, and Finland lets U.S. signals-intelligence aircraft use its airspace to monitor the Kola Peninsula, where the majority of Russia’s nuclear second-strike capability is concentrated. By preventing Russian dominance in the broader North Atlantic, Nordic cooperation has also advanced the 2025 U.S. National Security Strategy objective of maintaining—in cooperation with allies and partners—favorable balances of power in the world’s key regions.

There is every reason for Washington to treat the Nordic states as exemplary allies and endorse their advancements in regional cooperation. And yet the Trump administration’s approach to the region has been at best incoherent. On the one hand, U.S. officials have commended Nordic efforts to bolster defense spending—Denmark, Finland, Norway, and Sweden are all above or on track to reach three percent of GDP by 2029 and are committed to reaching the Hague target of five percent of GDP by 2035. On the other, U.S. President Donald Trump has repeatedly mused about taking over Greenland, a nightmare scenario for the Nordics that would pit their mutual solidarity against their respective relationships with the United States.

The Greenland agreement that Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk signed in September should encourage the Trump administration to play a larger, more constructive role in Arctic security. So far, Washington has treated defense spending as the key enabler of NATO 3.0. But a European-led alliance also needs allies that can use their growing capabilities as efficiently and seamlessly as possible. If the United States were to encourage and back Nordic-style minilateral latticework in other critical subregions, it would empower a more competent, capable, and commanding NATO 3.0.

The Greenland Deal Proves Self-Reliance Is Not an Option

#5936. California prosecutors slam Newsom's death row commutations, accuse governor of putting 'politics over people'

San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow accused Gov. Gavin Newsom of ignoring crime victims and violating the will of California voters following a sweeping announcement on death row commutations.

District attorneys and law enforcement unions across California have publicly condemned Gov. Gavin Newsom following his announcement to commute the sentences of 548 death row inmates, a decision one prosecutor called a slap in the face to victims' families.

Newsom’s sweeping order to commute the condemned inmates to life in prison without the possibility of parole has drawn intense criticism alongside praise from anti-death penalty advocates.

"I think it's all about politics, sadly. Politics is over people in this case, and that's a real sad state of affairs," San Luis Obispo County District Attorney Dan Dow told Fox News Digital.

ALABAMA GOVERNOR COMMUTES DEATH SENTENCE AS DOUBTS EMERGE ABOUT EVIDENCE IN MURDER CONVICTION

Law enforcement officials and prosecutors have criticized Gov. Gavin Newsom for issuing a blanket commutation for all of California's death row inmates. (Jane Tyska/Digital First Media/East Bay Times via Getty Images/Frazer Harrison/WireImage)

In an open letter detailing his decision, Newsom said California's capital punishment system is fundamentally at odds with the state's principles.

"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom wrote. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us."

POPE LEO DENOUNCES DEATH PENALTY AS 'INADMISSIBLE' AHEAD OF PENTAGON'S PLANNED LIVESTREAMED EXECUTION

Upon taking office in 2019, Newsom issued an executive moratorium on capital punishment. California has not carried out an execution since 2006.

The backlash to the governor's announcement was immediate.

FLORIDA PUTS 77-YEAR-OLD MAN TO DEATH FOR DEPUTY'S MURDER AS STATE CLOSES IN ON EXECUTION RECORD

"Justice will not have been served for these victims, dozens of them in San Diego County," said Lt. Jared Wilson, president of the San Diego Police Officers Association.

"Their last memories were of these evil, evil men who took their lives. What Gavin Newsom has done is awful."

Lt. Sam Robinson calls to open a door at San Quentin State Prison's death row in San Quentin, Calif., Aug. 15, 2016. The prison is California's oldest penitentiary and houses the state's only death row for men with 700 condemned inmates. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)

Wilson and other law enforcement officials strongly criticized the blanket clemency, citing cases like that of Jesse Michael Gomez, who was sentenced to death for the 2016 murder of San Diego police officer Jonathan "J.D." De Guzman.

"Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty, and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes," said Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman.

"Until the law is changed, my office will continue to evaluate every death penalty-eligible case with the rigor, care and restraint these decisions demand."

NEW YORK BILLS COULD ABOLISH LIFE WITHOUT PAROLE FOR SERIAL KILLERS AND COP KILLERS, CRITICS WARN

Orange County District Attorney Todd Spitzer called the commutations "mercy for the wolves … while inflicting the ultimate act of cruelty on the sheep," saying voters in California have upheld the death penalty in recent years.

Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco, who previously ran for governor, noted that 127 inmates on California’s death row were sentenced for crimes committed in his county.

"These sentences were not handed down without due process," he said. "They followed extensive investigations, lengthy trials, evidence presented in court and decisions made by juries and judges.

"Yet, with one sweeping executive decision, the governor has chosen to override those outcomes, disregarding the voices of victims’ families, the work of prosecutors and the pursuit of justice that took years to achieve."

College students Rachel Newhouse and Aundria Crawford were killed separately. Their killer, Rex Krebs, was sentenced to death for the brutal slayings. (San Luis Obispo County District Attorney)

Among the 548 inmates whose sentences were commuted are two men convicted in San Luis Obispo County: Michael Whisenhunt, 61, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 torture and murder of his girlfriend's 1-year-old daughter, Kesha Gurke; and Rex Krebs, 60, who was convicted in the brutal slayings of two female college students.

CHARLES MANSON CULT FOLLOWER BRUCE DAVIS, CONVICTED IN TWO 1969 KILLINGS, DIES BEHIND BARS AT 83

Dow noted that families of the victims were neither consulted nor notified prior to Newsom's public announcement.

"I was just sickened, frankly, for the crime victims in California who were slapped in the face by our governor," Dow said.

JUDGE BLOCKS ALABAMA'S NITROGEN GAS EXECUTION METHOD, RULES IT IS UNCONSTITUTIONALLY CRUEL

Addressing arguments from anti-death penalty groups who contend that capital punishment is inherently flawed and racially biased, Dow defended the current legal framework.

"We have a rigorous defense procedure that weeds out cases. I have strong confidence in the integrity of our convictions," he said.

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

#5934. Do the Democrats Have a Cohesive Economic Plan?

This issue is preventing our website from loading properly. Please review the following troubleshooting tips or contact us at [email protected].

Q&A: Do the Democrats Have a Cohesive Economic Plan?

Create an FP account to save articles to read later.

Downloadable PDFs are a benefit of an FP subscription.

Contact us at [email protected] to learn about upgrade options, unlocking the ability to gift this article.

Prefer to listen? To hear this entire conversation, and more episodes in the weeks ahead, follow Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts.

This week’s congressional elections in the United States saw a historic shift toward Democrats, who won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, including wins in traditionally red states such as Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina. But with President Donald Trump still in the White House and Democrats still trying to give shape to their own agenda, the implications for economic policy remain unclear.

Was the election outcome primarily fueled by inflation? What are the implications for the AI industry? And what macroeconomic options do the Democrats now have?

This week’s congressional elections in the United States saw a historic shift toward Democrats, who won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate, including wins in traditionally red states such as Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina. But with President Donald Trump still in the White House and Democrats still trying to give shape to their own agenda, the implications for economic policy remain unclear.

Was the election outcome primarily fueled by inflation? What are the implications for the AI industry? And what macroeconomic options do the Democrats now have?

Those are just a few of the questions that came up in my recent conversation with FP economics columnist Adam Tooze on the podcast we co-host, Ones and Tooze. What follows is an excerpt, edited for length and clarity. For the full conversation, look for Ones and Tooze wherever you get your podcasts. And check out Adam’s Substack newsletter.

Cameron Abadi: What is the relationship between a political event of this magnitude and mundane cost-of-living issues, which most Americans seem to have been bothered by? Is this the stuff that political tsunamis are made of?

Adam Tooze: The cost-of-living issue, and the continuous shocks of price increases and the felt experience of the exorbitant level of prices, has probably not been as pressing as it is in the current moment in many parts of the U.S. since the 1970s. So at that level, there’s a kind of epochal quality to this. And the other thing surely to say is that nor have we had a government, an administration and a supportive Congress, so blithely refusing to simply take seriously any of those issues in a meaningful way. And it’s that combination, I think, which creates this outcome. It would have been damaging to everyone’s sort of self-understanding as a rational political analyst if something like this outcome had not happened.

Because how can you have this level of dissatisfaction over prices and price increases and a government committed to protectionism, to starting a war, to incredibly unequal tax breaks, to promoting a growth model that is so K-shaped, that is so promoting a wealth inequality, and not get a backlash? That would have tested the ongoing debate about whether the ’90s formula, “It’s the economy, stupid”—this would really have put a stake through the heart of that theory with garlic on top if we had not seen this backlash.

CA: This kind of epochal shift inevitably sparks debates about new, or renewed, political taxonomies in the United States. The term that is now being used to describe many of the new senators and governors elected by Democrats in unlikely places is “prairie populism.” And I’m curious what that term might mean when it comes to economic policy?

AT: Going all the way back to the late 19th century, there has been a brand of radical, challenging, anti-status quo politics, in contrast to socialism, which was populism. Populism came out of the prairie, out of the Midwest of the prairie states of the agricultural constituency, because it was about the way in which the gilded age economy in the United States was rigged in the interests of coastal elites—basically New York and the East coast elite.

And that’s the echo that’s being picked up on in this sort of talk. It’s a little exaggerated because there’s a huge difference between present day consumer orientated cost of living type of politics and the sort of radicalism, the deep structural changes that late 19th-century populists were demanding—who were really challenging the fundamental structures of the American political economy of that moment. And I do think that’s one of the fundamental questions for the Democrats right now, is that coming out of the midterms of 2018—which were also a Democratic breakthrough, against the first Trump presidency, though not on the current scale—there was a real sense that the discourse of American politics shifted. You got figures like Jake Sullivan spiraling to the top of the democratic pile on an agenda that was an explicit break in neoliberalism.

And I don’t quite know where that goes right now, whether there is a mood on the large part of the Democratic Party to resume that kind of quite more fundamental questioning of the orthodoxies or whether we take all that for granted now and we’re going to just focus on trying to deliver. I think we haven’t quite got the bearings yet of what this victory means. It was predicted, but I haven’t so far seen on the part of the Democrats a kind of coherent, new, comprehensive agenda—even in the sense of defining what its limits would be and how far one wants to go—emerging at this point.

CA: Polls suggest that many voters in the United States share skepticism about artificial intelligence and the role it’s playing in the economy, specifically the proliferation of data centers. What is the future of AI potentially with this new Democratic-controlled Congress?

AT: It’s been quite something to behold, the anxiety running through Wall Street over the last couple of days and kind of climaxing last night about the potential threat to the data center build out. Because America’s path to the AI future is very compute heavy. It’s all about data center build outs. And if you look at the states where this is happening, apart from Virginia, Ohio, Pennsylvania, I think the central play is Texas. And there was a real lot of big tech money mobilized on this issue of trying to ensure that a group of AI friendly politicians were elected.

And on the contrary then, the groundswell of Democratic mobilization was around AI and data centers as kind of a bundling issue, right? It’s about local pollution from the noise and everything else. It’s about local electricity rates and the impact that these huge consumers have on local energy prices. And it’s about AI as AI, its direct role on the labor market. And it’s about AI as the symbol of an irresponsible, unanswerable kind of oligarchy that just stamps itself on the face of American society. And these were a very powerful combination.

And I think Wall Street analysts were counting 40 or 41 local referenda, local motions that are being passed. All of which I think went to the anti-AI side. And in Texas, we’re talking about 60 gigawatts of buildouts, so an absolutely gigantic buildout valued at $200 billion, I think. And now the Democrats have a much more powerful hold on Texas politics than any time recently. And as we know, in the regional political economy of the United States, Texas and Florida are two great red state counter-examples to the New York and California visions of America’s future. And so for this break to happen is really very dramatic.

And it does form a connection between this electoral result and the market. On the morning after the election, though the S&P 500 as a whole was doing fine, Tesla had sold off, CoreWeave, all of these cloud companies have sold off quite hard. Trump’s media platforms are down, unsurprisingly. So it does look as though there is a selective shakeout happening across stock that are very exposed on the AI issue, very exposed to this blowback and are, in any case, over the last couple of months, looking increasingly fragile from a financial point of view.

CA: Democrats are promising to make life for ordinary Americans more affordable, but how they’ll do that is still somewhat of an open question. On a macroeconomic level, could finding a way to lower interest rates be something that Democrats in Congress turn their attention to?

AT: I think this is a really interesting question. I mean, there’s a real tension between projects of trying to address the cost of living crisis through concrete interventions on particular prices and market structure and price gouging on drugs and microeconomic policy strategies and the bigger macroeconomic picture.

And of course, Congress doesn’t shape that bigger macroeconomic picture. Really except through fiscal policy. It doesn’t have a direct influence on interest rates. If it wants to see interest rates come down, the way to do that, presumably, would be to adopt tough fiscal policy. It doesn’t necessarily mean you slash spending, but you would need to raise taxes and you’d need to actually build a coalition that was willing to do that. And there’s lots of ways of doing that in a progressive way. But that’s not something the Democrats have been keen to do recently, really, is to push redistributional taxes. Or you have to put the Fed in a position where it has no option but to do various very unconventional interventions. Which again is perfectly logical and sensible from a left Keynesian point of view. But it’s a breach of the kind of orthodoxy which the Democrats have embraced all the time outside moments of absolute crisis.

So I do think this question of what the agenda of the Democrats is really, macroeconomically, is quite unclear. Because we’re clearly no longer in the Larry Summers Bill Clinton 1990s era. We left that behind in the Biden administration. What the agenda, what the paradigm now is I think is very open-ended. Take the issue of AI. One of the effects of the AI boom is to suck foreign money into the American equity markets. It’s one of the fundamental ways in which the American balance payments now currently balances. If that goes away—and there’s very good reasons for wanting to embrace that as American’s future, slow this down, try and close the two legs of the K-shaped economy—the most likely prediction is that the dollar depreciates, the dollar devalues.

And again, you’ll find people saying, Well, that will be great for industrial policy, that’s exactly what we need, American producers are more competitive, who needs tariffs if you have a devaluing dollar? But the dollar is also American purchasing power. And so if the dollar devalues appreciably, seriously, this raises the price of American imports. It raises the cost of buying foreign goods for American consumers. It isn’t a way to increase purchasing power and address the cost-of-living crisis. It does the opposite, right? It restricts imports by way of raising the price of foreign goods.

Now, this isn’t one-to-one or simple, but there’s just a series of tensions here that are not squarely addressed at the current moment. There hasn’t been any cause to address them, though I also think there was an agenda around the Biden administration that pretty clearly spelled out some of the trade-offs here. For instance, we would intentionally slow down the renewable energy surge in the U.S. because it involved Chinese solar panels and that wasn’t the top priority, actually.

So what are the new priorities? What is the new set? If the cost of living is the absolute priority over everything else, then you would think that a radical free trade agenda would be the way to go. But Congress can’t do that without a compliant White House. And which Democrat is actually going to run on that, given what we know the Biden administration did, which was to maintain Trump’s tariffs from the first administration? And big parts of the Democratic coalition, notably what’s left of the blue collar trade unions, are, shall we say, pro-tariff, broadly speaking. Not Trump’s crazy ones, but they are not interested in ensuring that American consumers can have the cheapest possible affordable family car. That’s not their agenda. So there’s a whole series of really quite complicated trade-offs here that will have to be faced again.
